name: Lydians
place: Sardis and the gold-bearing Pactolus, western Anatolia
desc: The people of Sardis, said by Herodotus to be the first to strike coins of gold and silver and the first shopkeepers. Their last king, Croesus, was so rich that his name still means wealth.
source: Herodotus, Histories book 1; excavations at Sardis (from 1910 and 1958), including its gold refinery

gluttonous: sold bread, oil and ribbons from a stall in the market
cautious: washed a fleece full of gold dust out of the Pactolus
devout: wove a cloth so fine the goddess's priestesses asked for it

inventions.name: Stamped Coins
inventions.source: Electrum coins stamped with a lion's head, Sardis, c. 630–600 BCE: among the first coins anywhere
inventions.desc: Lumps of gold-silver of a set weight, stamped with a lion so no one need weigh them: +2 mood, the stores hold 15 more, a little more lore.
inventions.hint: Needs the gold of the river, and someone who leads the trading.

inventions.name: Gold Refinery
inventions.source: A 6th-century BCE workshop at Sardis separated pure gold from electrum with salt in clay pots
inventions.desc: Pale gold heated with salt until the silver is drawn out and only pure gold is left: +2 mood, rites bring 5% more devotion.
inventions.hint: Needs river gold, salt and fire.

inventions.name: Dice and Knucklebones
inventions.source: Herodotus 1.94: the Lydians claimed to have invented dice, knucklebones and ball games to forget hunger in a long famine
inventions.desc: Games of bone and chance to pass the long evenings: +3 mood, and hunger is felt a little less.
inventions.hint: Comes from many evenings by the fire.

inventions.name: The Lydian Mode
inventions.source: Greek writers named a musical mode after Lydia, and Plato thought it too soft for warriors
inventions.desc: Sweet, slow songs for the feast: +3 mood, though the warriors grow a little soft.
inventions.hint: Comes from rites and evenings by the fire.

foods.name: Kandaulos
foods.source: A rich Lydian dish described by Athenaeus: boiled meat with bread, cheese, dill and broth
foods.desc: Meat, breadcrumbs, cheese and dill in a rich broth: hunger grows 10% slower, +2 mood.

foods.name: Honeyed Figs
foods.desc: Figs dried in the sun and kept in honey: +2 mood, food spoils 5% slower.

finds.name: Gold Sands of the River
finds.source: The Pactolus carried electrum dust down from Mount Tmolus, the source of Lydia's wealth
finds.desc: Glittering flakes in the river gravel, caught on fleeces laid in the stream.

finds.name: Wild Figs
finds.desc: Soft sweet fruit from trees that grow out of rock and wall.

people.name: Sandas
people.desc: He knows which bend of the river hides the most gold.
memory: found a nugget the size of a thumb in the river

people.name: Kawa
people.desc: She was selling in the market before markets had a name.
memory: sold out a whole cart of bread before noon

people.name: Gyges
people.source: Herodotus 1.8–14; Assyrian records name him 'Gugu of Luddi'
people.desc: A bodyguard who became king of Lydia; the Greeks told that he did it with a ring that made him invisible.

people.name: Alyattes
people.source: Herodotus 1.74; his huge burial mound at Bin Tepe
people.desc: The king who was fighting the Medes when the day turned to night, and made peace on the spot. His burial mound is one of the largest ever raised.

people.name: Solon
people.source: Herodotus 1.29–33 tells of his visit to Croesus; the dates make it doubtful
people.text: a grey-bearded traveller from across the sea, who looks at our treasures and seems unimpressed.
memory: told a king that no man can be called happy until he is dead
people.desc: The Athenian lawgiver, who in Herodotus' story warned Croesus that wealth is not happiness.

people.name: Croesus
people.label: Croesus, the Richest of Kings
people.desc: Gold flows to him. Trade 8, Lore 4.

people.name: Arachne
people.epithet: the Weaver Who Challenged a Goddess
people.label: Arachne the Weaver
people.desc: No loom in the world is finer. Crafting 8.

people.name: Gugu
people.label: Gugu of the Hidden Ring
people.desc: A shepherd who finds a ring of invisibility. Combat 7, Foraging 5.

events.title: The Battle of the Eclipse
events.source: Herodotus 1.74: in the sixth year of war between Lydia and Media, day turned to night during a battle (28 May 585 BCE), and both sides made peace
events.text: The war party was face to face with the enemy when the sun went black. Both sides stand frozen in the strange twilight, spears lowered.

options.label: Make peace under the dark sun

do.feat: Made peace when the sun went dark

options.result: The chiefs swear peace, and seal it with a marriage.

options.label: Charge while they are afraid
options.result: The warriors charge into the twilight. Some say the gods will remember it.

events.title: Eighteen Years of Hunger
events.source: Herodotus 1.94: in a long famine the Lydians ate only every other day and played games on the rest; at last half of them sailed west under Tyrrhenus and became the Etruscans
events.text: The harvests keep failing. The chief proposes: eat one day, play games the next to forget hunger. If that is not enough, half the people must go and find a new land.

options.label: Eat one day, play the next
options.result: Bones rattle in every hut. The hunger is still there, but it passes more quickly.

options.label: Send the young to find a new land
options.result: A band of young people sets out to the west and does not come back. Those who stay have more to eat.

events.title: Ask the Oracle
events.source: Herodotus 1.53: told that if he attacked Persia 'he would destroy a great empire', Croesus attacked, and destroyed his own
events.text: Before a great raid, the chief sends gifts to a famous seer. The answer comes back: 'If you march, a great people will fall.' The warriors cheer. The seer's messenger does not smile.

options.label: March!
options.result: The warriors march. Behind them, something circles the undefended camp.

options.label: Think again about which people
options.result: The chief stays home. Years later people still argue about what the seer meant.

tales.name: The Ring of Gyges
tales.text: A shepherd sheltering from a storm found a crack in the earth, and inside a bronze horse, and inside the horse a dead giant wearing a gold ring. When the shepherd turned the ring on his finger, he vanished from sight. He went to the palace unseen, and made himself king.
tales.moral: would you be just if no one could see you?

tales.name: Midas Washes Away the Gold
tales.text: King Midas wished that everything he touched would turn to gold, and his bread and wine turned to gold in his mouth. Starving, he begged the god to take the gift back, and was told to wash in the spring of the Pactolus. The gold flowed off him into the river, and its sands have glittered ever since.

tales.name: Arachne and the Goddess
tales.source: Ovid, Metamorphoses book 6: Arachne was a girl of Lydia
tales.text: A Lydian girl wove so well that she said even the goddess of weaving could not beat her. The goddess came and they wove side by side. Arachne's cloth was perfect, and it mocked the gods. In anger the goddess turned her into a spider, and she weaves still.

tales.name: Call No Man Happy
tales.text: The richest king showed a wise traveller all his gold and asked who was the happiest man alive. The traveller named a poor Athenian who died bravely for his city. Years later, on the pyre of his conqueror, the king cried out the traveller's name, and so his life was spared.
